There is no doubt that tire policy ot the government for some years past has been directed more especially toward getting people to go into western Canada rather than eastern Canada; perhaps it was because the government thought that eastern Canada was fairly well populated already, and that the east could look after itself. As a matter of fact, the results show that the east, in this respect at all events, could not look after itself without assistance from the federal government, because the bulk of the immigrants, practically all the immigrants that came to this country, went into the west. I think, now that the tide of immigration has set so strongly towards the west, that the government could afford for a few years to neglect that part of the country and turn its attention toward the east. If they did that for a few years, no doubt a sufficient number of people would still go into the west to meet the requirements of that part of the country, as many would go as could be perhaps assimilated. Now, it is generally (supposed that eastern Canada has a soil as fertile as that of the west. In my remarks I will confine myself to Prince Edward Island chiefly, as that is where I live. I cultivated a farm myself some years ago, about the ordinary size in Prince Edward Island, and I will tell you what it produced. I do this chiefly for the benefit of the Minister of the Interior, who lias most to do with the policy of immigration. I found I could produce from an acre of land about 300 bushels of merchantable potatoes, 800 bushels of other vegetables, such as turnips and mangles. I could produce from 30 to 35 bushels of wheat to the acre, about 50 bushels of oats, about 40 bushels of barley, from 3 to 4 tons of hay. I do not think the west could do much bet: ter than that. Of course, there is this . great .difference; in the east we have to ap-

ply manure to the soil in order to get these results, but I am informed they have not got to do that in the west at the present time. The time will come probably when they will be obliged to do that.
It is under ordinary conditions that we get these results. I am told that under better conditions much better results would be obtained. Dr. McPhail of McGill University who is now growing potatoes largely in Prince Edward Island has told me that he can get 500 bushels of merchantable potatoes from an acre of land and that he can produce that result by applying some $12 worth of commercial fertilizers and seeding down to clover every three Real's. Results like that, providing we had a market for the produce, must be profitable. We have about a million acres of land on Prince Edward Island, practically all cultivable, and providing one fifth of that was devoted to the growing of potatoes under Dr. McPhail's plan, there would be nothing like a market in Canada [DOT]aind we would have to look for a market abroad. There is no doubt that if we had access to the New England states for that article, at all events, it would be a very great advantage to us. It may be asked: Why acre we losing our population in the eastern provinces, particularly in Prince Edward Island where the soil is so fertile, when we can produce such abundant crops. There is no doubt that we are losing population and it appears to me that our young people will leave us anyhow. Some years ago it was considered that perhaps farm work was more laborious, that it was more -shall I call it, degraded?-and that an equal degree of credit could not be obtained from work of that kind as that which could be obtained by work in a profession or some other occupation of life. The young people therefore were lured to the states. Since the west has been opened up the lure of the west has drawn our young people away. They are going away and, in my judgment, they will continue to go. Many of our young people have gone to the United States and as a rule they have done well and the reports that come back induce others to go. They have gone to the cities of Canada and to the west and they have done well. Farm help has become so scarce that it is very difficult to operate a farm in Prince Edward Island. When the young people go away and the older people find they cannot get farm help they simply have to sell the farms or leave them and for these reasons there are a number of vacant farms in Prince Edward Island that may be purchased cheaply. I think that perhaps similar conditions prevail in other provinces. If the Minister of the Interior could obtain farmers in the British Isles or in northern Europe with a small amount of capital, with even
$2,000, accustomed to farming, such people might settle in Prince Edward Island with a considerable degree of safety. If they had $3,000 or $4,000 so much the better. You can purchase cultivated farms with buildings in a fair state of repair for from $15 to $50 per acre. I sold a farm I had with good outbuildings at $30 an acre largely because it was almost impossible to get farm help. There is a good field for young men and women who would be disposed to go upon the farms as farm help. There is a good field for a reasonable number of men from -the old country who had a small amount of capital and would like to settle in a country such as the eastern provinces rather than go to the west. I do not think efforts have been made in the past to get that class of people to come to Canada. The men who have been brought to the west have gone out there to farm upon a large scale, but the small farmer, the man who is accustomed to a mixed farming and who perhaps would wish such under established conditions, would be an acquisition and if this class is obtainable every effort should be made to get it. I believe our young people will leave us anyhow, and the only way to get the farms occupied is by getting men from the British Isles and Northern Europe. If that could be done it would be a great advantage. There is no doubt that Prince Edward Island would support a population three times as large as that which we have now. We have now something over 90,000. Some few years ago we had over 100,000. I think that is unfair. If something could be done to compel the railways to bring back the young men and women who wanted to come back at the same rate as they took them out west it would he only just and fair. A number of our people leave us on these cheap

harvest excursions and do not return. They are induced by the railways to do that, and chiefly by the Canadian Pacific railway. I wish to make these few remarks for the benefit of the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Rogers) or for those who will have this matter under consideration. There is plenty of room for the right kind of immigrant in eastern Canada, and particularly for farmers with small capital and farm labourers. We are very much in need of that class of people. Whatever the Minister of the Interior or the government can do towards that end will be greatly appreciated in the east and will help to build up the whole of Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. A. McLEAN (Queens, Prince Edward Island).
Hon. ROBERT ROGERS (Minister of the Interior).
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Before making any reference to the subject matter of the resolution introduced by my hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes), I would like to say a word or two with reference to the remarks which have fallen from some hon. gentlemen who spoke after him. In the first place, let me say to my hon. friend the member for Westmorland that I heard with Mr. M'LEAN (Queens, P.E.I.)
some surprise-his statement to the effect that in the immigration office in the city of London, England, we have no representative who knows anything at all about Nova Scotia or the maritime provinces. Let me say to him that if, when I make inquiry, I find that he is correct in his statement, I shall take the earliest possible opportunity of seeing that we have in that important office men who have thorough knowledge .and <are able to speak intelligently regarding the possibilities end resources of every province in our Dominion.
I am not going to attempt at this late hour to follow the hon. gentleman in his discussion of that old question of reciprocity, which, so far as the people of Canada are concerned, is dead and buried for all time to come. I cannot agree with the proposition of the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) that in view of the present conditions it would not be wise to invite immigrants to the maritime provinces. As the minister presiding over the Department of the Interior, I propose to invite immigration to the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island in the same form and manner and with the same hope of results that I do to the other provinces of this Dominion, believing as I do with an intense conviction that we have in the maritime provinces, in common with the other provinces of Canada, great possibilities which should attract immigrants who want to better their condition. As a result of that great National Policy which was laid down many years ago, and which has been adopted and followed by both parties in this Dominion from that day to this, we are in the proud position in Canada of being able to point to the fact that we have more desirable conditions for intending immigrants than those which can be found in any other country in the world. Therefore, it becomes my duty as the minister of that department to lend every energy I possess to the work of carrying out a policy such as I believe will be best calculated to increase our population to the advantage of those who come as well as for the upbuilding of the country. Now, I have taken careful note of the remarks of my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean), and I shall be glad to Teeeive the representations which he proposes to make, and I can assure him that they will receive full, clear and faithful consideration at the hands of the department. I have also taken very careful note of the suggestions which my hon. friend from the St. Lawrence division (Mr. Bicker-dike) has made for certain amendments in the regulations. I am not clear at the moment whether the changes which he

recommends would be advisable and desirable at the present time, but I shall be glad to give them the consideration which they require. In respect to the resolution itself, I entirely agree with the statements which have been so clearly placed before this House by the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes). When I took charge of the Department of Immigration I at once saw, from an examination of the records, that in my judgment some improvement could be made in that department, and I found that that improvement could be best made by a policy of co-operation with the different provinces. To that end an officer was engaged, whose duty it was to visit the different provinces, and I am glad to say that that work is meeting with good results. I have had as a result of that course a visit from the Premier of British Columbia and one or two of his colleagues, and they are in a most hearty manner cooperating with us with respect to immigration to that province. I have also had a visit from a representative of the government of Ontario in the person of Mr. Duff, the Minister of Agriculture, and I am glad to be able to inform this House that I have been able to arrange a policy of co-operation with the great province of Ontario under which we are not going to duplicate our work, as we have done in the past, but are going to work together in harmony, and by this means are going to accomplish greater results for immigration in that province in the future than has ever been done in the past. I also had the pleasure of meeting the Premier of the province of New Brunswick and his Attorney General, and discussed with them the policy that they propose to inaugurate, better calculated to bring immigration to that province. I am very much encouraged by the aggressive policy which Mr. Fleming and his colleagues propose to adopt in connection with [DOT] the work in New Brunswick. I have made an arrangement with them by which we propose to assist them largely in their aggressive policy, and I am satisfied that as time goes on very fruitful and very desirable results will be found to come from the arrangements which we have made in this connection, and which I believe will be announced by the Premier of New Brunswick in the very near future. We have invited every province of the Dominion to co-operate with us, and every province will receive fair and generous treatment at the hands of this government.
Adopting, as we have, a policy which we believe to be that calculated to advance the best interests of our common country, a policy that will be common to all the
provinces of Canada, I do not desire in speaking of our immigration, to know either eastern Canada or western Canada. Let me say to those who have spoken this afternoon that we are going to inaugurate a policy by which we shall give publicity to every province in Canada. The gentlemen from the maritime provinces have pointed out in very able .addresses the great possibilities which those provinces possess, possibilities which in themselves are inviting to intending immigrants in many, respects; and it becomes our duty, as the central government, to advertise these advantages to the people of the world, in order that the maritime provinces in common with the others, may secure all advantages, and in order that the attractions which they possess may be presented to the intending immigrants from all parts of Europe, the United States, and elsewhere, who desire to become citizens of our Dominion.
Now, we have only to look at the returns of immigration in Canada during the last year, to find that the immigration to the three maritime provinces was less, I believe, than one third of the immigration secured by any other province in this Dominion. In view of this condition, I say, I am not surprised that we should have the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes), and other hon. members in this House from the maritime provinces, bringing to the attention of this parliament and of the people of the country, the advantages they .possess in those provinces. In view of the fact, they claim that the maritime provinces have not been getting their share of immigration. And the evidence of the correctness of their statement is to be found in the figures to which I have just referred. I am not here to say, nor am I in a position to say, what the reasons are that they have not secured a greater increase than that which I have named. But I am here to say, as representing the Department of Immigration, and voicing the policy of the government of the day, that we propose a policy of cooperation with all the provinces, to lend every assistance in our power, to give to the maritime provinces, and the other provinces all the support and all the assistance which a very healthy treasury is able to give, in order to bring immigration to Canada, with a view to having here a happy and contented people in greater, and much greater, numbers than we have at this time.

Mr. Speaker, I do not desire to criticise the resolution or to find fault with the policy of the Department of Immigration^ as laid down by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Rogers). But inasmuch as a large part of the remarks offered to the House this after-

noon and evening have practically been in criticism of the previous administration of the department, it would, hardly be in place for me to let the occasion pass without having something to say in regard to that administration and policy. The hon. members who have preceded me said frequently that they wanted a Canadian policy, a policy that would build up Canada. Well, I take it that Canada has been built up with a fair degree of rapidity during the past few years under the immigration policy that has been followed. When we consider the increase in the population of Canada during the past few years-increasing, remember, from year to year until the year which has just closed has shown the largest immigration that ever took place in the history of this country-and in view of probably a larger percentage of increased population than has ever occurred in the history of any other country in the world, it might be thought that a policy having such success might have received commendation rather than adverse criticism. The policy which achieved such results was not by any means a haphazard policy. And let me suggest further that a policy on the lines which have been suggested by the larger number of our friends who have spoken here tonight, could not by any possibility have achieved such success for this Dominion of Canada. Some of our friends who have spoken seem to think that immigration is a matter of finding the people in one place, picking them up and removing them to some other place. I do not think my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Rogers) is under any such impression. But I can assure the House that if he is, or if his colleagues are under that impression, they will find they are greatly mistaken. The first requisite of successful immigration effort is opportunity for the immigrants. I will admit that advertising is valuable; and the evidence given here today proves that the advertising efforts under the late adminstration were reasonably successful, and, I presume correspondingly satisfactory. But advertising alone will not make successful immigration effort. It assists. But the original foundation of success is opportunity for the immigrant. Unless you have the_ opportunity, you cannot get the immigration by all the advertising expenditure you see fit to make. It was because of the opportunities in western Canada that the immigration to western Canada has been so much larger in proportion than that to other portions of Canada, and not because of the advertising. So far as the advertising is concerned, I will just say for the information of the House, that the most important piece of immigration literature gotten out by the Interior Department during my administration was an atlas of Canada which gave every province in Can-Mr. OLIVER.
ada equal treatment both in maps and in descriptive matter. This atlas is used in schools not only in many parts of Canada, but in foreign countries as well, notably in Belgium. It is also used in schools largely in England. And in that .atlas the maritime provinces had practically the same consideration in proportion to area and population as the western provinces had. Again, a very large sum of money was spent in maps-' school maps ' as they were called- which gave, of course, a complete view of the whole Dominion without partiality to one section or another.
Also when delegations have come out from the old country at the instance of the Interior Department to look over Canada to see what opportunities there were, they toured the maritime provinces just as well as the prairie provinces, and reported upon the opportunities they found there. Besides that, special pamphlets have been got out to describe particularly the advantages of the maritime provinces. I do not question for a moment the possibility of larger efforts, toeing made in the future th an have been made in the past. I do not find any fault with such efforts, I wish them all success, and believe they will achieve some success. But I say that if the department, in the past ten years, had directed its main efforts and its main expenditures to securing settlers for the eastern provinces, the results to Canada would not have been in any measure such as they have been under the policy that has been pursued. It is not in the nature of the case possible, and it will not be possible in the future, should it ever be attempted; and I give the Minister of the Interior credit for too much common sense ever to attempt such a policy. The result of the policy that has been pursued in securing the - occupation and development of western Canada has been essentially and truly a Canadian policy, because it has been upon the successful development of western Canada, so far as that development has yet gone, that the prosperity and progress of this whole Dominion has been built. Its increase in cultivated land and in the number of farms occupied, in the products of the soil of those western provinces, has stimulated manufacturing enterprises in all parts of eastern Canada, and in no part more than in the very town of the hon. member for Cumberland, the town of Amherst where he resides. The town of Amherst depends very largely for its progress and prosperity on the settlement and development of western Canada. Of course, I give every credit to the enterprising men of Amherst who have established manufacturing enterprises in that city. But all the enterprises that could have been centred in Amherst, with all the ability of her business men, could not have succeeded were it .not for the development of the

great Northwest, and the cultivation of the wheat fields of that country.
Now a lament has been made of the loss of population in the maritime provinces. From one point of view I must say that I have no sympathy with it. If the maritime provinces have not increased in population as fast as other parts of the Dominion there is a reason for it, a reason not to the discredit of its people, but rather to their credit. They are an active and energetic people, who look for opportunities wherever they may be found, and they seize the best that can be found, whether they be far or near. It is just because they have looked for wider and better opportunities than existed at home that the population of the maritime provinces has not increased, because the people have gone elsewhere where they could do better. It is immeasurably to the benefit of Canada as a whole that the population ol the maritime provinces, instead of congesting there during the past five, ten or twenty years, has been spread far and wide over the whole Dominion. If the lack of increase of population was due entirely to the movement of the people of those provinces to western Canada, I say again that the maritime provinces are to be congratulated instead of being condoled with.
Unfortunately the natural increase of population in the maritime provinces, which I am given to understand is more than ordinarily rapid, has not been retained in those provinces. This is a fact to be deplored. I believe that a very large proportion, very much more than fifty per cent, has gone to the United States. This has been greatly to the advantage of the United States, and correspondingly to the disadvantage of Canada. If previous governments had established active agencies in the maritime provinces to secure a movement of people for the prairie west of Canada, fifteen or twenty years ago, would not Canada have been better off to-day, and would not the maritime provinces themselves be just as well, or better off? I say it is little less than a crime to have allowed so many young men of those provinces to go every year to the United States, while not a finger was raised to prevent that exodus. It would have been ten times better for the government of Canada to have entered upon an active immigration campaign in those provinces in order to create a movement of their people to the prairies of the west instead of to the United States. Canada would have been far, far ahead, not only in money, but in men, in prestige, and in national spirit as well. I bad the pleasure of attending a dinner in Boston on the 24th of May last, a dinner given by the Intercolonial Club, and I was appalled, Mr. Speaker, at the figures that were given me of the number of people of lower province birth who were resident in the city of Boston, in the state
of Massachusetts, and in the other New England states. If I remember right, I was told that there were not less than 30,000 people of maritime province birth permanently resident in the city of Boston, and over 100,000 in the state of Massachussetts. There is no doubt that they form a very important element of the population of the city of Boston, and of the state of Massachussetts. I say it is most unfortunate that this should be the case. The late government was so impressed with that condition of affairs that we established an immigration agency in the city of Boston for the express purpose of getting back some of the maritime province people, and directing them to our prairie west. We achieved some success, and I am sorry to read in the newspapers that the present administration has seen fit to close the office. I think it was doing valuable work, and more valuable work could have beeen done. I believe that a very considerable movement could have been secured of those people toward our northwest. A moderate movement had already been started, and I believe it would have increased with time. Now let me put this thought before our friends.
It is not to the interest of Canada that a man who has good abilities shall be kept in an environment where he cannot use those, abilities to his own advantage or to the advantage of the country. With respect to the man who is born, we will say, in Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island or New Brunswick in that condition of life that does not give him a farm to cultivate or a business to conduct, and who must spend his time in those provinces an employee of some other person, surely it is to the interest of Canada that that man, by removing to our Canadian west, becomes a proprietor land a producer on a large scale and adds enormously to the productive wealth of the country year by year. Is it not to the benefit of the country as well as to the individual himself, that instead of only securing a livelihood in Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island or New Brunswick, by taking advantage of the opportunities which exist on the prairies, lie is able to become a producer on a large scale, and become, we will siay, a man of wealth and substance? Surely it is to the good of Canada that this change should be made as well as to the good of the man himself. I do not sympathize witb the view that would restrict the people of the maritime provinces, Quebec or Ontario, to the limited opportunities of those provinces when the greater opportunities of the western provinces are available to them. I want it to be distinctly understood that I have no word of discredit for the maritime provinces, or fox Ontario and Quebec, or the opportunities that exist there. Probably there are no more beautiful coun-

tries in the world. Probably there is no country where the advantages are greater, but if the initial advaintagea of this country have been occupied:, if (they have been, 'absorbed by the population Which has been resident there for ia series of generations', it is reason and common sense that the same opportunity does not exist there for the recent generation that does exist in a country that still lies vacant and is open to the first man who takes advantage of it. That is the situation and that is why the population in the west has increased and why the population in the maritime provinces 'and Ontario and Quebec has not increased. It is for the good of the country that the opportunities of the western provinces are taken .advantage of by Canadians as much as possible. It would have been a misfortune for Canada if these opportunities had not been taken 'advantage of by Canadians and Canadians could not stay at home in the eastern provinces and still take advantage of them. There is nothing to regret because they have availed themselves of them. The only regret is that the people of eastern Canada, in so many thousands, have gone to the United States; have added their population and their wealth and their energy to that country and that these have been lost to Canada. Over a million of our people, born in Canada, are to-<diay in the United States instead of in our own northwest building up our own country.
I do not wish to introduce any controversial matter, but I think the references of the hon. Minister of the Interior as to the results of what he was pleased to call the National Policy were scarcely unfortunate under these conditions when we consider that under the rule of that policy, when it was in its fullest blast, was the time when we lost most of our people, when they transferred themselves from this *country to that. We lost them and our rivals gained them. The hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) went into a good deal of detail as to the administration of immigration, matters in the province of Ontario and he found some fault with the attitude of the Dominion Department of Immigration. I do not know how his discourse struck other members of the House but when my hon. friend stated that he himself was an officer of the Ontario government administering matters, it struck me that from the amount of complaint that he was able to make and the readiness with which he found matter to complain of there would naturally *be some difficulty for another government to give any administration within the sphere of his influence that would be satisfactory to him. May I just suggest here that this is one of the difficulties that my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior Mr. OLIVER.
will have to deal with if he desires to co-operate with the provincial governments in regard to immigration effort.. I wish him all success, but I must say that any efforts of ours to co-operate with the provincial government of Ontario were not met with any spirit that tended to success and co-operation as the House might very well judge by the remarks of the hon. member for South Oxford. I do not wish to trouble the House with the details of the matter, but when we did the best we could to secure immigration of a desirable character to Ontario, we did not find the administration of the government of Ontario at all sympathetic or showing any apparent desire to co-operate with us in the effort. I hope the present minister will have more success in this line than I had. But, I would draw the attention of the House to the fact that in his mention of the interviews that he had with the different premiers of the different provinces his interviews so far were restricted to the premiers who were of the same political persuasion as himself, and did not happen to include the public representatives of the different provinces of a different political persuasion. There might be some difficulty in working out the problem on that line.
They are all coming around now.

Well, I suppose that is tlie object. Until they do come around 1 think possibly there might be some little difficulty such as we had the misfortune to find in Ontario. I will not trouble the House with the details of our little difficulties in Ontario. We did the best we could and we believe that the immigration effort that we put forth in Ontario did have a good effect. But, we were quite aware of the limitation of our work and we would be very glad to see that work carried on with better results than we were able to 'achieve. Possibly with cordial cooperation between the Dominion and provincial governments better results can be achieved.
I want to say one word now in regard to the suggestion of the hon. member for Montreal, St. Lawrence (Mr. Bickerdike) in which he objects strongly to the financial restriction which is placed upon immigration. That financial restriction was not placed until there appeared to be the very greatest urgency and necessity for it. The financial restriction was placed upon immigration, and I do not think there is any doubt or that there can be any question that the improvement which we have secured in the standing and character of the immigrants who have come during the past few years, notwithstanding the tremendous increase in their numbers, is very largely due to the financial requirement

as well as other methods of selection and restriction.
I do not think it is possible in this day and generation to have a successlul immigration policy satisfactory to the people of this country unless it is selective and restrictive. It is true cases of hardship arise and it is true that in the past many have landed here who did not have twenty-five or fifty dollars, but the times have changed and I say it here now, and I say it strongly, that in my judgment a restrictive and selective immigration policy is an absolute necessity in this Dominion, and a financial requirement from the immigrant is one important feature of such a policy. I have no objection whatever to the resolution, but I must warn its mover (Mr. Rhodes), that he is too sanguine if he expects that any amount of government effort or government expenditure will achieve the same success in the maritime provinces as has been achieved in regard to the prairie provinces where the opportunities are greater.
Does not the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver), think that the immigrants should be examined at the port of embarkation.

The people have been kind enough to relieve me of the responsibility of administering the Immigration Department, and I do not think it important that I should give my opinion on that matter. However, I may frankly state that my view is that parliament having laid down the rule that immigrants shall not be admitted to Canada unless they meet certain physical and financial requirements, it is the duty of the government to carry out that law. It is a responsibility on the steamship companies that they shall not bring to our shores passengers who are not able to meet the requirements we have laid down, and if we took on ourselves the responsibility of holding an examination on the other side of the _water, we would be taking on our shoulders a responsibility that the circumstances did not call for, and we would not be any further ahead in protecting the immigrants. We have not jurisdiction outside of our shores, but the steamships have jurisdiction in the ports whence they sail. They hav" a nominal medical examination at these ports, and if they make that nominal medical examination practical there will be no trouble about it. I do not think it is a sound policy for Canada to undertake a medical examination on the other side of the Atlantic. In my judgment our immigration policy is best carried out by the methods pursued up to the present time.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver), did not touch the real question.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member (Mr. Bickerdike), has already spoken.

I just wish to point out that there is no doubt we could get a law passed allowing examination before embarkation and although there might be extra expense it would be worth money. If my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) realized the great hardship experienced by these families which are broken up, he would recommend the new Minister of the Interior to change the existing law.

The steamship offices have their own medical officers and make an examination in the country from which the vessel sails, and if that examination is effective, it is all that is required, and if it is not effective, the steamship companies suffer the loss of taking the immigrants back again. I do not think the responsibility of this country goes any further than that. While I would not find any fault with the present Minister of Interior if he should order an examination on the other side, we will be borrowing trouble without achieving any good results.

Motion agreed to.
